standard_prerequisites.name: Turing computability and reductions
standard_prerequisites.statement: A problem is decidable when some Turing machine decides it; if one problem reduces to another by a computable transformation and the target is decidable, so is the source.
standard_prerequisites.use: The whole proof is the reduction from the decision problem for validity to satisfiability (source lines 1542-1555).

standard_prerequisites.name: Validity versus unsatisfiability of the negation
standard_prerequisites.statement: A first-order sentence is valid if and only if its negation is unsatisfiable.
standard_prerequisites.use: This equivalence is what converts the answer of the assumed machine S into an answer for the decision problem (source lines 1552-1554).

standard_prerequisites.name: The decision problem for validity is unsolvable
standard_prerequisites.statement: There is no Turing machine that decides whether an arbitrary first-order sentence is valid.
standard_prerequisites.use: The derived machine would solve that problem, and the proof closes by contradiction (source lines 1554-1555).

core_obligations: Assume a Turing machine S that decides satisfiability and describe a machine that would decide validity: write the input sentence, shift it, and prefix the negation symbol, using that these are computable tape operations (source lines 1542-1545).
Run S on the negated sentence and convert its yes/no answer into a stroke or a blank on square 1, so that the output is 1 exactly when the negation is unsatisfiable (source lines 1547-1551).

Use that a sentence is valid exactly when its negation is unsatisfiable to conclude that the constructed machine decides validity, contradicting the known unsolvability of that decision problem, so satisfiability cannot be decidable (source lines 1552-1555).

proof_roadmap.step: Assume a satisfiability decider S and build the front end that negates the input sentence.
Run S on the negated sentence and encode its answer as a stroke or blank on square 1.
Identify the resulting machine as a validity decider via the validity/unsatisfiability equivalence and contradict unsolvability.

difficulty_reason: The counted unit is the author's own corollary cor:undecidable-sat at source lines 1537-1539: it is undecidable whether an arbitrary sentence of first-order logic is satisfiable. The proof at source lines 1541-1556 is a reduction that has to be assembled step by step. It assumes a Turing machine S deciding satisfiability and then describes a machine that would decide validity: copy the input sentence, write a negation symbol in front of it, run S on the negated sentence, and translate the answer back, using that a sentence is valid exactly when its negation is unsatisfiable. The description is given at the level of tape operations (moving the sentence one square, returning to square 1, writing the negation, inspecting square 1 for a stroke, erasing or writing one), so the reader has to accept that these are computable operations and that the resulting machine halts on every input. The contradiction is then with the already established unsolvability of the decision problem for validity. Nothing in the statement names the reduction or the two closure facts it uses. No result outside the retained text is used.
